words.definition: Lasting only a very short time before fading away.
words.example: The evanescent glow of the fireflies vanished the instant I reached for them.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ever-vanishing' — evan-ESCENT slips off like vapor escaping the air.

words.definition: Existing or continuing for only a brief period of time.
words.example: Fame in that industry proved transitory; last year's stars are already forgotten.
words.mnemonic: Think 'transit' — like a train passing through a station, it doesn't stay.

words.definition: Continuing or recurring again and again through the years.
words.example: Complaints about parking are a perennial topic at every neighborhood meeting.
words.mnemonic: Per + ennial (annual) means 'through the years' — perennial flowers bloom every spring.

words.definition: Continuing forever or without any interruption.
words.example: The toddler kept up a perpetual stream of questions from dawn until bedtime.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'perpetual motion machine' that spins on and never stops.

words.definition: Going on and on without any pause, especially something irritating.
words.example: The incessant dripping of the faucet kept me awake all night.
words.mnemonic: In + cease + ant = 'not ceasing' — the ants that never stop marching.

words.definition: Continuing steadily without ever coming to an end.
words.example: The ceaseless roar of the waterfall drowned out every attempt at conversation.
words.mnemonic: Cease + less — 'less ceasing', so it simply never ceases.

words.definition: Seemingly without end, especially because dull or tiresome.
words.example: The professor's interminable lecture left half the class asleep at their desks.
words.mnemonic: In + terminable = 'cannot be terminated' — no terminal, no exit, no end.

words.definition: Made to last longer than expected or necessary.
words.example: After protracted negotiations spanning three months, the two sides finally signed.
words.mnemonic: Pro + tract (to pull) — like a tractor dragging something out ever longer.

words.definition: Continued for a greater length of time than usual.
words.example: A prolonged drought left the reservoir at its lowest level in decades.
words.mnemonic: Pro + long — literally something that has been 'made long'.

words.definition: Continuing steadily over a long time without weakening or changing.
words.example: She had an abiding love of the sea that never once left her.
words.mnemonic: From 'abide' — to dwell and bide your time; it stays put and remains.

words.definition: Continuing to exist or last over a long period.
words.example: Their friendship proved enduring, surviving decades apart on different continents.
words.mnemonic: En + during — it keeps going 'during' every hardship thrown at it.

words.definition: Able to withstand wear and last a long time without breaking.
words.example: These boots are durable enough to survive years of rugged mountain hiking.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'durare' (to harden) — the root in 'endure'; built to take a beating.

words.definition: Originating so long ago that no one recalls the beginning.
words.example: The villagers have fished these waters since time immemorial.
words.mnemonic: im- (not) + memorial (memory) — stretching back beyond anyone's memory.

words.definition: Too old-fashioned to be useful in the present day.
words.example: The office still relied on antiquated fax machines while rivals had gone fully digital.
words.mnemonic: Antique + -ated — turned into an antique that belongs in a museum.

words.definition: Belonging to a much earlier era and no longer in common use.
words.example: Legal documents are full of archaic words like 'hereinafter' and 'whereof'.
words.mnemonic: Share the 'arch-' of 'archaeology' — digging up something very, very old.

words.definition: No longer in use because something newer has taken its place.
words.example: Floppy disks are now obsolete, replaced by cloud storage and tiny USB drives.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'obviously so late' — it showed up too late and got left behind.

words.definition: Something that existed or happened before another thing.
words.example: Jazz was a clear antecedent of the rock music that dominated later decades.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ante' (before) + 'cedere' (go): the thing that goes before.

words.definition: All the people who will live in future generations.
words.example: She saved her grandmother's letters for posterity, so her descendants would know their history.
words.mnemonic: Think 'posterior' (behind/after) — the ones who come after us.

words.definition: Belonging to an earlier time; existing in the past but not now.
words.example: My erstwhile business partner now runs a rival company across town.
words.mnemonic: 'Erst' is German for 'earlier' + 'while' (time): from an earlier time.

words.definition: In an early stage and just starting to appear.
words.example: The doctor caught the incipient infection before it could spread through her body.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'inception' — the very start of something.

words.definition: At a very early and undeveloped stage.
words.example: The startup's plans were still embryonic, sketched on napkins with no funding yet.
words.mnemonic: Think 'embryo' — an unborn baby: something in its earliest form.

words.definition: New, inexperienced, and still in an early stage of growth.
words.example: The fledgling airline owned just two planes and flew to only three cities.
words.mnemonic: A fledgling is a baby bird just growing its feathers to fledge — brand new at flying.

words.definition: Growing or expanding quickly and flourishing.
words.example: The city's burgeoning tech scene attracted thousands of new workers every month.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bursting' — a bud bursting open and shooting upward.

words.definition: To sprout, or for an idea to start to take root and develop.
words.example: The seeds germinate faster if you keep the soil warm and moist.
words.mnemonic: Think 'germ' — a tiny seed of life beginning to grow.

words.definition: To gradually decrease in size, strength, or intensity.
words.example: As the party dragged past midnight, the guests' energy began to wane.
words.mnemonic: The moon wanes — it grows smaller and thinner each night.

words.definition: To move back or slowly fall away in amount or strength.
words.example: The tide began to ebb, leaving wet sand and stranded starfish behind.
words.mnemonic: Ebb tide flows OUT — the 'e' pulls away from shore, like the sea retreating.

words.definition: To gradually become smaller in amount or number.
words.example: Their savings dwindled until only a few coins remained in the jar.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'diminish' shrinking down — dwindle whittles away to little.

words.definition: To become less intense, or to sink to a lower level.
words.example: Once the medication worked, the swelling in his ankle slowly subsided.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' (down) + 'side' — it settles down and sits lower.

words.definition: To move back or withdraw from a previous position.
words.example: As the floodwater receded, families returned to inspect their damaged homes.
words.mnemonic: 'Re' (back) + 'cede' (go): to go back — like a receding hairline.

words.definition: To stay somewhere longer than expected, or be slow to disappear.
words.example: The smell of woodsmoke lingered in her coat long after the campfire died.
words.mnemonic: Linger sounds like 'longer' — you hang around for longer.

words.definition: To stay in one place longer than needed, or be slow to leave.
words.example: Don't tarry at the gate; the train leaves in two minutes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tar-y' — imagine your shoes stuck in tar, keeping you from leaving.

words.definition: To keep delaying a task you should be doing, usually out of reluctance.
words.example: He would procrastinate all evening, cleaning his desk instead of writing the essay.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-crastinate' from Latin 'cras' (tomorrow) — you're a pro at pushing things to tomorrow.

words.definition: To move an event or action to a later time.
words.example: Heavy rain forced them to postpone the outdoor wedding until next month.
words.mnemonic: 'Post-' means after — you place the event after its original spot on the calendar.

words.definition: To waste time idly or move without any sense of urgency.
words.example: The children dallied by the pond, poking sticks in the mud instead of coming home.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'rally' — but instead of rallying to act, you dally and drift.

words.definition: Said of time, to go by or pass gradually.
words.example: Three hours seemed to elapse before the doctor finally called her name.
words.mnemonic: 'E-lapse' — think of a 'lap' on a clock face ticking away as time slips past.

words.definition: A brief failure, slip, or gap in something normally maintained.
words.example: A momentary lapse in concentration caused him to miss his exit on the highway.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'gap' where you 'let it slip' — l(et)-a-p(s)e, a small break in the flow.

words.definition: Starting and stopping repeatedly rather than staying constant.
words.example: The intermittent buzzing of the faulty light made it hard to concentrate.
words.mnemonic: 'Inter-mit' — like an intermission that keeps interrupting, on and off, on and off.

words.definition: Happening at scattered, irregular times with no clear pattern.
words.example: Only sporadic gunfire broke the silence, never at any predictable moment.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spores' scattered by a mushroom — landing here and there, randomly.

words.definition: Happening at regular, evenly spaced intervals of time.
words.example: The nurse made periodic checks on the patient, exactly every hour on the dot.
words.mnemonic: Think of 'period' as a fixed stretch of time — it repeats each period, like the periodic table's rows.

words.definition: Following a repeating pattern that returns to its starting point.
words.example: The economy is cyclical, swinging from boom to bust and back to boom again.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'cycle' — a bicycle wheel turning round and round to the same spot.

words.definition: Coming back again and again over time.
words.example: A recurrent nightmare of falling woke her almost every week.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-current' — the current keeps flowing back, returning like a repeated event.

words.definition: Occurring in separate, occasional bursts rather than steadily.
words.example: His interest in the piano was episodic, flaring up for a week and then vanishing for months.
words.mnemonic: From 'episode' — like a TV series, it comes in distinct installments, not one continuous stream.

words.definition: Lasting a very long time or constantly returning; long-term.
words.example: Her chronic back pain had troubled her every single day for a decade.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'chronos' (time) — like a 'chronicle,' it stretches on and on through time.

words.definition: To cause something to continue indefinitely or keep it alive.
words.example: Repeating the old rumor only serves to perpetuate a myth that was never true.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'perpetual' — you make it perpetual, keeping it going forever.

words.definition: To make a process happen faster or more efficiently.
words.example: Paying the extra fee will expedite your passport so it arrives within three days.
words.mnemonic: Think 'express delivery' — an 'exped-ition' that gets your feet moving quickly toward the goal.

words.definition: To do something quickly or to make an event happen sooner.
words.example: She hastened down the platform when she heard the train's doors beginning to close.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'haste' plus '-en' — haste means speed, so to hasten is to add speed to something.

words.definition: To make something move or happen faster, or to increase in speed over time.
words.example: As the traffic light turned green, she pressed the pedal to accelerate onto the open highway.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-cellar-ate' — imagine racing so fast you 'ate' up the road all the way down to the cellar.

words.definition: To cause an event to happen suddenly or sooner than expected.
words.example: A single careless remark precipitated a quarrel that split the family for years.
words.mnemonic: Think 'precipice' — pushing something off a cliff makes it fall suddenly, just as you precipitate an event.

words.definition: About to occur very soon or at any moment.
words.example: Dark clouds massed on the horizon, and the sailors knew a storm was imminent.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in a minute' — something imminent is arriving in a minute.

words.definition: Looming or approaching, often with a sense of threat.
words.example: The memo about layoffs filled the office with a sense of impending doom.
words.mnemonic: Root 'pend' means to hang (as in 'pendant') — something impending hangs over you, ready to drop.

words.definition: Coming or happening later than it should have.
words.example: He sent a belated birthday card a full week after the party had ended.
words.mnemonic: It literally hides 'late' — be-LATE-d means made late.

words.definition: Arriving or occurring after the expected time.
words.example: The teacher marked him tardy again when he slipped in after the bell had rung.
words.mnemonic: Picture wading through sticky 'tar' — it would drag you down and make you slow and late.

words.definition: Occurring before the right, natural, or expected time.
words.example: Celebrating the win at halftime proved premature when the other team scored twice.
words.mnemonic: 'pre-' means before plus 'mature' means ripe — premature is before ripeness.

words.definition: Happening at an awkward or inappropriate moment, or too soon.
words.example: His untimely joke during the funeral left everyone shifting uncomfortably in their seats.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' (not) plus 'timely' (well-timed) — the opposite of well-timed.

words.definition: Happening at a favorable or especially suitable moment.
words.example: The reporter's question came at an opportune moment, just as the minister let his guard down.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside 'opportunity' — an opportune time is when opportunity knocks.

words.definition: Lasting only for the span between two events; provisional.
words.example: The board named an interim director to run the company until a permanent hire was found.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'inter' means between — the interim is the stretch in between.

words.definition: Arranged for the present and likely to be changed later.
words.example: The peace deal was only provisional, pending approval by both parliaments.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'provision' — a provisional plan is a stopgap provision until the real one arrives.

words.definition: Lasting for a limited period and not permanent.
words.example: The bridge closure is only temporary; crews expect to reopen the lanes by Friday.
words.mnemonic: Root 'tempor' means time (as in 'tempo') — it lasts only a little time.

words.definition: Lasting only a brief instant before passing.
words.example: There was a momentary flicker of the lights before the power steadied again.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'moment' — it lasts just a moment.

words.definition: Existing or occurring at the same time as something else.
words.example: The judge ordered the two sentences to run concurrent, so he served them together.
words.mnemonic: 'con-' (together) plus 'current' — two currents running together at once.

words.definition: Occurring or existing at the same moment in time.
words.example: The two sprinters crossed the line in a simultaneous burst, and judges needed the photo to separate them.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'simul' means together — SIMUL-taneous events all happen together in the same instant.

words.definition: Belonging to or produced during the same stretch of time as something else.
words.example: The diary and the soldier's letters are contemporaneous, both written inside the same besieged city.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + tempor (time) — sharing the same time, like two 'temporary' things running side by side.

words.definition: Having the same age, date, or origin as another thing.
words.example: These granite peaks are coeval with the earliest dinosaurs, thrust up in that same ancient age.
words.mnemonic: co- (together) + 'ev' from Latin aevum (age) — of one shared age.

words.definition: Coming or happening after something else in time or order.
words.example: The first meeting was frosty, but every subsequent one grew a little warmer.
words.mnemonic: sub- + sequ (to follow, as in 'sequence') — it follows along behind.

words.definition: Following afterward, often as a direct consequence of what came before.
words.example: A wire sparked, and in the ensuing panic everyone forgot exactly where the exits were.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-suing' — one event 'sues' and the next comes chasing right after it.

words.definition: Occurring at last as the final result of a process or wait.
words.example: Years of quiet saving led to her eventual purchase of the little farmhouse.
words.mnemonic: Picture a long DMV line: your number is EVENTUAL — it truly comes, but only at the very end.

words.definition: Coming immediately before the last one in a series.
words.example: On the penultimate page she finally guessed the killer, just one chapter shy of the reveal.
words.mnemonic: pen- from Latin paene ('almost') + ultimate — almost the ultimate, so next-to-last.

words.definition: The length of time that something continues or lasts.
words.example: For the duration of the storm, the ferries stayed roped to the dock.
words.mnemonic: dur- from Latin durare ('to last') — how long a thing endures.

words.definition: A gap of time or space between two points or events.
words.example: The tower bells rang at regular intervals, one chime every quarter hour.
words.mnemonic: inter- (between) + 'val' from vallum (rampart) — the open space between the walls.

words.definition: A particular period in history marked by notable events or features.
words.example: The printing press opened a new epoch of learning that spread across Europe.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'EP-ick' — an epoch is an EPIC stretch of time worth carving into stone.

words.definition: A long, distinct stretch of history sharing one character or spirit.
words.example: The fall of the wall marked the end of an era split by rival ideologies.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'aura' — each era carries its own distinct aura, a whole age with one mood.

words.definition: A critical point in time, especially where a decision must be made.
words.example: At this juncture, with the funds nearly gone, the founders had to choose: sell or fight on.
words.mnemonic: junct- (join, as in 'junction') — a juncture is the joining point where roads and choices meet.

words.definition: The point at which something begins or a critical level is reached.
words.example: Standing at the threshold of adulthood, she felt both eager and afraid.
words.mnemonic: It's the strip you step over in a doorway — cross it and you enter what lies beyond.

words.definition: The beginning or early stage of something, often unwelcome.
words.example: At the first onset of fever, she cancelled the trip and climbed into bed.
words.mnemonic: on + set — the moment things are 'set on', switched on and starting to move.

words.definition: The start or founding moment of a plan, institution, or activity.
words.example: The club has welcomed dogs since its inception in 1920, the very year it was founded.
words.mnemonic: in- + cept (from capere, 'to take') — the taking-hold point where it all begins; recall the film planting an idea at its very start.

words.definition: The point at which something begins.
words.example: From the outset of the trip, everyone sensed it would end in disaster.
words.mnemonic: You SET OUT on a journey — the outset is where you start.

words.definition: The act or moment of beginning something.
words.example: A trumpet fanfare signalled the commencement of the royal ceremony.
words.mnemonic: 'Commence' means to begin — even graduation is called this because a new life begins.

words.definition: The highest or climactic point reached after a long process.
words.example: Winning Olympic gold was the culmination of twenty years of daily training.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'culmen' means summit — picture reaching the very peak of a mountain.

words.definition: A complete stopping or halting of some activity.
words.example: The sudden cessation of gunfire let medics rush toward the wounded.
words.mnemonic: 'Cease' + 'station' — the station where all activity ceases.

words.definition: A gap or break in the continuity of something.
words.example: The band went on a three-year hiatus before touring again.
words.mnemonic: HIGH-AY-tus — say it and your mouth gapes open, just like the gap it names.

words.definition: A short period of rest from something difficult or unpleasant.
words.example: The shade of the oak gave the hikers a welcome respite from the blazing sun.
words.mnemonic: REST + a little bite — a small bite of rest during hardship.

words.definition: A brief period of calm or quiet in noise or activity.
words.example: During a lull in the conversation, she quietly slipped out the door.
words.mnemonic: A LULLaby quiets a baby — a lull is that same calm hush.

words.definition: An intervening stretch of time between two events or stages.
words.example: The picnic was a pleasant interlude between two exhausting meetings.
words.mnemonic: INTER (between) + LUDE (Latin 'ludus', play) — a little play staged between the acts.

words.definition: A scheduled pause between parts of a play, film, or concert.
words.example: We bought ice cream during the intermission before the second act began.
words.mnemonic: INTER + MISSION — a break in the middle of the show's mission.

words.definition: An officially declared temporary ban on some activity.
words.example: The council imposed a moratorium on new building near the flooded river.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'mora' means delay — a moratorium presses pause and says 'more delay'.

words.definition: A small trace or sign left by something no longer present.
words.example: A single crumbling tower was the only vestige of the medieval fortress.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'vestigium' means footprint — a faint footprint left by the past.

words.definition: An object that has survived from an earlier time.
words.example: The museum displayed a rusted relic recovered from a sunken warship.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'relinquish' — something left behind and surviving from long ago.

words.definition: A small piece left over after the rest is used or gone.
words.example: She stitched a colorful quilt from remnants of her children's old shirts.
words.mnemonic: 'Remain' is hidden inside — a remnant is what remains.

words.definition: Matter that stays behind after a process or removal.
words.example: A sticky residue coated the pan long after the syrup had boiled away.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'reside' — it's what resides and stays put after everything else leaves.

words.definition: The distant past, especially the era before the Middle Ages.
words.example: Scholars of antiquity spend their careers studying Greece and Rome.
words.mnemonic: ANTIQUE + ity — the age of antiques, the very old world.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — time and duration
